item.title: bdnews24.com Editor Toufique Imrose Khalidi passes away
item.description:
Toufique Imrose Khalidi, editor-in-chief and publisher of leading online news portal bdnews24.com, has died in London on Friday.
He breathed his last at around 7:00pm (Bangladesh time) on Friday while undergoing treatment at a London hospital, a senior bdnews24.com journalist confirmed to Dhaka Tribune.
According to his colleagues, Khalidi had travelled to London recently for medical treatment. He reportedly became dizzy and collapsed in his hotel room on Thursday night. He was subsequently taken to hospital by ambulance, where doctors declared him dead at around 7:00pm.
“Doctors said he had suffered a brain haemorrhage,” his colleagues said.
Khalidi had served as the publisher and editor-in-chief of bdnews24.com, the online news outlet and news agency he owned, since 2006.
He worked at the BBC in London as a presenter, producer and editor.
In December 2017, Khalidi received the National ICT Award in recognition of his contribution to the development of Digital Bangladesh.

item.title: Altercation at the airport: DB arrests Major (retd) Akhtaruzzaman
item.description:
The Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Detective Branch (DB) has taken Jamaat-e-Islami leader and former MP Major (retd) Akhtaruzzaman into custody following an altercation at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
“DB has taken him into custody,” confirmed DB Additional Commissioner Shafiqul Islam.
Asked about the situation, he said: “DB personnel are at his house. He will accompany them once he finishes his prayers.”
A case has been filed against Jamaat leader Major (retd) Akhteruzzaman over allegations of creating disorder at the airport, obstructing government officials in performing their duties and physically assaulting an on-duty security officer amid a shortage of luggage trolleys.
Airport security officer Md Shahriar Alam Sajib filed the case with Airport Police Station on Friday under several sections of the Penal Code.
According to the case statement, a shortage of luggage trolleys and delays in baggage delivery occurred around 10:40am on October 1 at baggage belt No 8 due to heavy passenger pressure following the arrival of a flight (BG-338) from Madinah.
As tensions among passengers escalated, Airport Executive Director Group Captain SM Ragib Samad went to the spot at the request of Dhaka-5 MP Mohammad Kamal Hossain.
The statement alleges that while the executive director was trying to calm the situation, Akhteruzzaman approached him aggressively and verbally abused him. He allegedly threatened the official, saying, “I will beat you up” and “I will throw you out by the neck.”
He also allegedly made highly offensive remarks about the civil aviation and tourism minister. The situation reportedly worsened when protocol assistants accompanying Akhteruzzaman began recording videos on their mobile phones inside the airport’s restricted Key Point Installation (KPI) area.
When security supervisor Warrant Officer Mohammad Kamal Uddin asked them to stop recording, Akhteruzzaman allegedly became angry, verbally abused him and physically assaulted him.
He is also accused of throwing bottles of holy Zamzam water collected by passengers from trolleys, damaging them, and behaving aggressively towards a representative of Biman Bangladesh Airlines.
The complainant said Akhteruzzaman’s actions obstructed government officials from performing their duties at the sensitive and restricted facility, threatening to disrupt normal airport security and order.
The case was filed under Sections 186, 189, 294, 323, 352, 353, 504 and 506 of the Penal Code on allegations of obstructing public servants, causing hurt, using criminal force, intentional insult and criminal intimidation.
Airport Police Station Officer-in-Charge Kamrul Hasan Talukder confirmed the filing of the case, saying an investigation was underway.
Asked whether Akhteruzzaman would be arrested, the OC said, “We cannot say anything about that at this stage. Since a case has been filed, we will investigate the matter and take necessary legal action.”

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,114 as four die in 24 hours
item.description:
Four more children have died from measles and measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Friday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,114.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified three of the latest casualties as suspected and one as a confirmed measles death.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,012, while the number of confirmed deaths rose to 102, as one new confirmed measles death was reported in the last 24 hours.
The three new suspected fatalities were all recorded in the Dhaka division, specifically within the Dhaka district.
A total of 1,221 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Friday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 194,084.
During the same period, 21 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 21,623.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 172,021 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 166,933 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS 2 oct.png report.

item.title: 7 killed as bus hits autorickshaw in Mymensingh
item.description:
Seven passengers of a CNG-run auto-rickshaw were killed after it was hit by a bus in Mymensingh on Friday afternoon.
The accident occurred around 1:15pm in the East Gandhrapa bypass area of the city.
Four of the deceased have been identified as Minan, 5, son of Kabir Hossain of Dari Hamidpur in Jamalpur Sadar upazila; Rashida Begum, 80, wife of Majum Ali from the same village; Mofazzal Hossain Lebu Mia, 54; and his daughter Marjina, 25.
Efforts are underway to identify the remaining 3 victims.
Confirming the deaths, Mymensingh Kotwali Model police station Officer-in-Charge Shibirul Islam said a Rajib Paribahan bus travelling from Dhaka to Jamalpur collided head-on with a CNG-run auto-rickshaw coming from Muktagachha.
Additional Superintendent of Police Abdullah Al Mamun confirmed that all 7 victims died at the scene. The accident occurred when the Jamalpur-bound bus collided head-on with the auto-rickshaw coming from the opposite direction in the Gandrapa area of Mymensingh Sadar.
The auto-rickshaw was badly damaged in the collision.
Police and Fire Service personnel reached the scene after receiving the information and recovered the bodies. Traffic movement on the road was disrupted after the accident but has since returned to normal.
The Rajib Paribahan bus and the auto-rickshaw involved in the accident are in police custody. Necessary legal procedures, including preparation of the inquest reports of the deceased, are underway.
Traffic movement on the road is currently normal.

item.title: Four remanded over extortion, blank firing in Bangla Motor
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Friday placed four people, including expelled Jubo Dal leader Ferdous Ahmed Saimon, on remand in a case filed over allegedly beating a man and firing blank shots after he refused to pay Tk50,000 in extortion in Bangla Motor area.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Israt Jahan passed the remand order after a hearing in the afternoon, granting 4 days’ remand for Saimon, the prime accused, and 3 days each for the other 3 accused.
The other accused sent to remand are Omar, 32, Morshed, 25, and Md Shaon, 25. SI Arif Reza of the prosecution department confirmed the matter.
He said there was no lawyer present for the accused during the remand hearing.
Earlier on Friday, SI Md Nasim, investigation officer of Hatirjheel police station, produced the accused before the court and sought 7 days’ remand for each in the interest of a proper investigation.
According to the case statement, at around 7:15pm on Thursday, October 1, the accused stopped plaintiff Md Sohan in front of a house in the New Eskaton area of Bangla Motors under Hatirjheel police station.
The case statement alleges that prime accused Ferdous Ahmed Saimon demanded Tk50,000 in extortion from him. When Sohan refused to pay, Saimon allegedly pulled out a pistol, pointed it at his chest and attempted to shoot him.
At one point, Saimon allegedly struck Sohan on the head with the butt of the pistol, while the other accused also beat him. The accused left the scene after people nearby approached.
The injured Sohan received first aid at a local pharmacy. Later, while he was travelling for further treatment, his brother-in-law Md Moktar Hossain joined him.
At that time, Saimon and the other accused allegedly arrived at the scene on motorcycles and again attempted to beat Sohan. Moktar Hossain was also allegedly beaten when he tried to intervene, according to the case statement.
The remand application states that Saimon fired 3 blank shots from the pistol at that time. Local people then chased and detained several of the accused.
Saimon was also detained when he attempted to flee. Police from Hatirjheel police station went to the scene after being informed and took them into custody.
Later, victim Md Sohan filed the case with Hatirjheel police station.
The remand application further states that preliminary investigation found the arrested accused to be active members of an organized extortion and criminal group.
The application said the accused needed to be interrogated on remand to identify the identities and whereabouts of others involved, arrest absconding accused and recover other information related to the case.
The police remand application also stated that the arrested accused have several drug cases filed with Hatirjheel and Kalabagan police stations.

item.title: Bangladesh urged to strengthen capacity to secure biodiversity funding
item.description:
Bangladesh needs to strengthen its institutional capacity and develop internationally viable projects to secure funding for biodiversity conservation, as experts warn that financial constraints remain a major obstacle to protecting the country’s rich natural ecosystems.
The issue is expected to feature prominently at the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17), scheduled to be held in Yerevan, Armenia, from October 19 to 30, 2026.
Despite its rich biodiversity, Bangladesh continues to face challenges in protecting forests, wetlands, rivers, coastal ecosystems and marine habitats. Habitat destruction, pollution, encroachment and climate change are putting increasing pressure on the country’s natural resources.
Experts say Bangladesh has conservation strategies and access to international funding mechanisms, but it needs to improve its ability to prepare and implement projects that meet international standards.
Dr Md Golam Rabbani, director of the Centre for Climate Change and Environmental Research (C3ER) at BRAC University, said the CBD has fewer financial resources than the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).
Unlike climate finance, which includes dedicated mechanisms such as the Green Climate Fund and the Adaptation Fund, biodiversity conservation has fewer dedicated funding channels.
However, Bangladesh can access funding through the Global Environment Facility (GEF), as well as programmes supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
Bangladesh has been actively accessing its country allocation from the GEF, but experts say more needs to be done to mobilize international resources for conservation.
Dr Rabbani said Bangladesh has the potential to expand its conservation areas to cover up to 30% of its territory, subject to political commitment and the availability of resources.
He stressed that securing international funding requires more than identifying conservation needs.
Bangladesh must develop bankable projects that meet international standards and strengthen its institutional and human resources to implement them effectively.
Bangladesh has 60 protected areas covering approximately 818,247 hectares, according to figures provided for this report.
These include 19 national parks, 13 Ecologically Critical Areas (ECAs) and five marine protected areas and reserves—four marine protected areas and one marine reserve.
While the country has taken steps to expand its conservation network, experts say the effectiveness of these areas depends on proper management, adequate financing and sustained implementation.
Expanding protected areas alone will not be enough to safeguard biodiversity. Conservation efforts must also address habitat degradation and the pressures faced by local communities that depend on natural resources.
SM Munjurul Hannan Khan, executive director of Nature Conservation Management (NACOM), said Bangladesh’s rich biodiversity provides an opportunity to attract international support.
Although the country is relatively small, it contains important biodiversity hotspots and ecosystems that have global conservation significance.
However, Bangladesh has yet to achieve significant success in mobilizing international funding for biodiversity conservation, he said.
He stressed the need to secure resources to implement the country’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP).
Bangladesh has already developed several strategies and plans, including the NBSAP and management plans for Ecologically Critical Areas. The challenge now is to mobilize the necessary financial and technical support to implement them.
According to Munjurul Hannan Khan, COP17 is not expected to allocate funds directly to individual countries. Instead, the conference will focus on discussions about financial mechanisms and ways to support member states in implementing their biodiversity commitments.
He expressed hope that the conference would make progress on resource mobilization mechanisms and support programmes for countries working to protect biodiversity.
For Bangladesh, the conference offers an opportunity to highlight its conservation priorities and seek stronger international cooperation.
Experts say the country should use the global platform to raise the need for financial assistance, technical support and institutional capacity-building.
Rivers and wetlands are essential to Bangladesh’s biodiversity, providing habitats for fish, aquatic plants, birds and other wildlife. However, pollution, encroachment and disruptions to natural water flows are threatening these ecosystems.
Mohammad Monir Hossain, chairman of the Bangladesh River Foundation, said protecting rivers and wetlands is essential to biodiversity conservation. He stressed the need to prevent pollution and encroachment, address unplanned development and restore the natural flow of rivers.
Experts say Bangladesh’s success in biodiversity conservation will depend on how effectively it translates existing policies and strategies into action.
Developing viable projects, improving institutional capacity and ensuring transparent implementation will be crucial to accessing international funding.
COP17 could provide an important platform for Bangladesh to press for greater financial and technical support. However, the country will also need to strengthen its own systems to ensure that available resources lead to measurable conservation outcomes.
With biodiversity under growing pressure, experts say sustained investment in protected areas, forests, rivers, wetlands and marine ecosystems will be essential to meeting Bangladesh’s conservation goals.

item.title: Ilish prices jump by Tk300 per kg in Chandpur
item.description:
Reduced ilish supply in Chandpur markets towards the end of the season has pushed prices up by Tk200-300 per kg within a week, with traders attributing the increase to lower supplies from rivers and the sea.
On Friday, October 2, a visit to Chandpur Boro Station Fish Landing Centre found a large number of buyers from different parts of the country. However, fish supplies had declined somewhat, with 1kg ilish selling for Tk2,500-2,600, 700-800g ilish for Tk2,000-2,200 per kg and 400-500g ilish for Tk1,500.
Shabe Barat Sarker, general secretary of Chandpur Boro Station Fish Traders Cooperative Society, said ilish supply had been comparatively low from the beginning of the current season.
He said: “Supply increased somewhat last month, bringing the price of ilish down to Tk2,100-2,200 per kg. However, supply has declined again over the past few days. Around 25 maunds of ilish arrived at Boro Station Fish Landing Centre on Friday, which is very low compared to demand. As a result, prices have increased by Tk200-300 per kg.”
Trader Alam Khan said a 22-day ban to protect mother ilish will begin on October 8. Many fishermen who went to sea have already started returning, so he does not expect supplies to increase or prices to fall in the coming days.
Abdur Rahman, a fisherman from Baharia in Chandpur, said very little ilish is now being caught in the rivers of Chandpur.
He said: “Although the presence of fish increased for a few days, we have to pack up our nets and boats before the ban. However, we will not go to the river during the government ban to protect mother ilish.”
Another fisherman from the same area, Sarwar, said it had become difficult to run his household as catches had declined.
He said: “It has become difficult to run the household because fewer fish are being caught. Although expenses have increased, we are not getting fish accordingly.”
District Fisheries Officer Fakhrul Islam said preparations had been completed to enforce the 22-day ban from October 8 to October 29 to protect mother ilish.
He said the period had been considered important for ilish breeding based on research, prompting the ban.
Ice factories will remain closed for the 22 days of the ban, and no dredging machines will be allowed to operate in the rivers, he said. Special monitoring will also be maintained to prevent fishermen from outside Chandpur from fishing in the rivers.
He also said there were plans to close the mouths of 8-9 important canals in the sanctuary areas. Police would set up checkpoints on important roads, while quick response teams would remain ready to take immediate action if any problems arose during operations.

item.title: 3 injured as lift falls at government housing project in Mirpur
item.description:
Three people were seriously injured after a lift fell to the ground at a government housing project for officials and employees in Dhaka's Mirpur on Friday morning.
The injured were identified as former Prime Minister's Office employee Mostafizur Rahman, 62, Nais Ahmed, 40, and his eight-year-old son, Md Wasi.
The accident occurred around 6am at Building 1 of the project, west of the Paikpara Ansar Camp in Mirpur-1.
The injured were rescued and taken to the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopaedic Rehabilitation (NITOR) in Agargaon.
Md Shahabuddin Ahmed, general secretary of the building and a personal officer at the Bangladesh Public Service Commission Secretariat, said the three residents of the fifth floor entered the lift after Fajr prayers.
Shortly afterwards, the lift reportedly broke loose and fell to the ground with a loud bang.
Hearing the noise, the building's security guard went to the scene and heard the injured people calling for help from inside the lift.
Several people from the surrounding area later helped rescue them and took them to hospital.
Mehedi Hasan, duty officer at Mirpur Model police station, said police had learned about the incident through several sources and sent officers to the scene.

item.title: Fourteen Chhatra League activists sent to jail after remand
item.description:
Fourteen leaders and activists of the banned Chhatra League, arrested from the house of former Barguna-2 MP Shaukat Hasanur Rahman Rimon, were sent to jail after completion of their remand.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Albiruni Mir passed the order on Friday, October 2, following an application by the investigation officer.
SI Helal Uddin of the prosecution department confirmed the matter.
The accused sent to jail are Md Yakub Hossain Rajib, Arafat Mia, Rifat Hawladar, Hridoy Hasan, Fahim, Rajib Hossain Rana, Md Firoz, Md Arif, Md Omar Faruk, Abdullah Al Aman, Sohanur Hossain Shahin, Md Hasib and Hasib Mia.
On Monday at around 7pm, police conducted a raid at the house of the former Barguna-2 MP and arrested 15 people, including the 14 accused. The following day, a court granted 1-day remand for Farzana and 3-day remand for the other 14 accused.
Farzana was sent to jail after completion of her remand on Wednesday.
On Friday, investigation officer SI Iqbal Hossain of Uttara West police station produced the 14 accused before the court and sought their detention in jail.
Helal Uddin said: “Bail petitions were filed for 11 accused. There was no bail petition for 3. The court rejected the bail petitions of the 11 and then ordered all 14 to be sent to jail.”
According to the case details, workers of the banned Chhatra League, Jubo League and Swechhasebak League allegedly gathered at the house of former Barguna-2 MP Shaukat Hasanur Rahman Rimon in Sector 7 under Uttara West police station in the capital and prepared to commit anti-state offenses and terrorist activities with the aim of destabilizing the state and destroying state infrastructure.
After receiving the information, police conducted a raid after 5pm on Monday and detained the accused from inside a room. At the time, 20-22 unidentified accused allegedly fled the scene.
During a search, police seized 20 pages containing the names and biographical details of 20 candidates for positions in the Kakchira Union Committee of Swechhasebak League’s Patharghata upazila unit in Barguna district from inside a drawer of a table in the room.
During questioning, the detained accused said they were members of the banned Chhatra League of Uttara West police station.
A case was filed at Uttara West police station under the Anti-Terrorism Act in connection with the incident.

item.title: Dengue: One more die as 1,163 hospitalized in 24 hours
item.description:
One person died of dengue and 1,163 were hospitalized after being infected with dengue in the last 24 hours till 8am on Friday, according to a regular report of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of the newly hospitalized dengue patients, 420 were in Dhaka Division, 77 in Mymensingh Division, 333 in Chittagong Division, 111 in Khulna Division, 151 in Barisal Division and 71 in Rangpur Division.
According to the report, a total of 82,761 dengue patients have so far been hospitalized across the country this year. With one death in the past 24 hours, the death toll from the disease stood at 250 this year.
However, in the last 24 hours, 1,163 patients recovered and were discharged from hospitals. This year, a total of 76,861 dengue patients have recovered and returned home after receiving treatment in hospitals.
A total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and 413 people died from the disease last year.

item.title: Vinicius-led Brazil take on India in historic Kolkata friendly
item.description:
Carlo Ancelotti’s star-studded Brazil are ready to take centre stage in Kolkata on Saturday when they face India for the first time in a senior international fixture.
The Brazil coach said Friday his team held respect for hosts India ahead of the historic friendly.
Five-time world champions Brazil will field a star-studded squad featuring Vinicius Junior for the game at Kolkata's Salt Lake Stadium on Saturday.
India, ranked 138th in the world, will face Brazil's senior men, ranked fifth, for the first time -- and on the back of a 1-1 draw with 44th-ranked Panama.
"We have respect for the quality of the Indian team," 67-year-old Ancelotti told reporters on the eve of the game.
"They played a good draw against Panama. We have full respect for our opponents."
Cricket-crazy India have never qualified for a World Cup, but football remains hugely popular -- especially in Kolkata and the southern city of Kochi.
"Cricket is part of their culture; football is not the most important game," said Ancelotti.
"But that doesn't mean they don't love football. We are happy to be here and show our quality to all who have the possibility to watch the game, and it will be a fantastic night."
Brazil will be without Raphinha, who withdrew with a thigh injury.
But their squad features top names, including Paris Saint-Germain captain Marquinhos and the Arsenal duo of Gabriel Magalhaes and Bruno Guimaraes.
Brazil are coming off a win and a draw against Australia from a friendly double-header and are looking to rebuild following their shock exit to Norway in the World Cup round-of-16 in July.
"It's true that we were not able to compete enough in the World Cup," said Ancelotti.
"It was a difficult period for us. It is motivation for a new generation of players to be able to compete at the highest level in the coming years."
"All these games in Australia and India are a good preparation and a good opportunity to show what we can do," the Italian added.
Brazil captain Marquinhos said the team's strong fan base in India was an added motivation.
Indian and South Asian fans are often divided in their football loyalties between Brazil and Argentina.
"India, outside Brazil, is one of the countries where there is the biggest support and fanbase for the entire squad," said Marquinhos.
India coach Khalid Jamil grinned as he took the stage after Ancelotti, and the two hugged for the photographers.
"Pressure will be there, but we have to handle that and take responsibility," said Jamil. "If you give your best, anything can happen."

item.title: City confirm appeal after Premier League charges verdict
item.description:
Manchester City confirmed on Friday that it had launched a "comprehensive appeal" after an independent commission ruled the club had broken Premier League financial rules.
The Premier League announced on Tuesday that an independent commission had found the Abu Dhabi-backed club guilty on more than 100 charges.
The 10-time English champions, who have always vehemently denied wrongdoing, said in a statement on Friday they had lodged an appeal on Thursday -- a day before the deadline.
"Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7:00 pm (1800 GMT) on Thursday 1st October 2026 the club lodged its comprehensive appeal against the opinion of the Premier League commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter," the club said.
"The club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.
"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.
"We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete."

item.title: Bangladesh women secure maiden Asian Games hockey win to finish ninth
item.description:
Bangladesh women’s hockey team finished ninth in the Asian Games after edging Singapore 2-1 in a penalty shootout in the ninth-12th place playoff at Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium in Japan Friday.
The match ended 1-1 in regulation time before Bangladesh held their nerve in the shootout to secure their first victory of the tournament.
Bangladesh made an attacking start and took the lead in the 10th minute through Irin Akter Riya, who scored a field goal to put the Tigresses ahead.
The Bangladesh side maintained their 1-0 advantage until half-time, but Singapore increased the pressure after the break in search of an equaliser.
Bangladesh were reduced to 10 players in the 42nd minute when Lima Akter received a yellow card and was temporarily suspended.
Singapore capitalised on their numerical advantage two minutes later, with Tou Li Min converting a penalty corner in the 44th minute to restore parity.
Neither side managed to find a winner in the remaining minutes, forcing the contest into a penalty shootout.
Bangladesh then prevailed 2-1 in the shootout to seal ninth place, bringing their Asian Games campaign to a close with a victory.
The result also marked a positive end to Bangladesh’s maiden women’s hockey campaign at the continental multi-sport event, following their earlier 3-3 draw against Kazakhstan that earned them their first-ever Asian Games point.

item.title: FA says Man City case has major implications for soccer integrity
item.description:
The Football Association said Friday that a ruling against Manchester City over major financial violations has significant implications for the integrity of soccer and that it is reviewing the decision.
An independent commission found Manchester City guilty of artificially inflating its revenue by more than $1 billion over nearly a decade through what the Premier League described as “sham” sponsorship agreements linked to the club’s ownership.
The commission found City guilty of all charges involving serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules between 2009 and 2018. It also found the club guilty of most of the charges related to its failure to cooperate with the investigation.
The FA, the governing body of English soccer, issued its first response to the biggest disciplinary case in Premier League history.
“The independent commission's decision has significant implications for the integrity of the game,” the FA said.
“We are carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate.”
The FA said it would “continue to monitor developments closely” but would not make further comments while the proceedings remain ongoing.
Manchester City has said it will appeal the ruling, which was published Tuesday. The deadline for filing the appeal is Friday.
The club’s potential punishment will be considered separately in a confidential hearing before the independent commission. Possible sanctions include a fine, points deduction or even expulsion from the Premier League.

item.title: India: Women fear for safety as sexual assaults surge
item.description:
Reports of the gang rape of a 17-year-old girl in New Delhi earlier this week has thrust the issue of women’s safety in India back into the spotlight.
Three men who posed as police officers took the girl away at gunpoint to a secluded part of the Aastha Kunj Park, according to local media.
Security around New Delhi’s parks has been stepped up since the incident, with a focus on improved lighting, increased security and more frequent patrols.
Anita Kunwar, an 18-year-old college student from city’s East Delhi district, said a lot has changed after what happened at Aastha Kunj Park.
“Women and girls across the city are incredibly wary, anxious, and deeply concerned about their safety,” she told DW. “An incident like this, especially in a public space where people go to relax, shatters your sense of security.”
“Reports of these ghastly sexual assaults seem to have risen in recent years,” said Deepika Singh, a university student in New Delhi. “It is as if these crimes are being normalized. It is sickening.”
“The assaults have also become more brutal and aggressive,” the 19-year-old told DW. “But I am not going to change the way I live my life because of them.”
Hundreds of students, many of them women, marched in New Delhi a few days after the alleged assault, demanding greater safety in public spaces.
“Our body is our own,” some placards read, while others demanded ​freedom to go out at night without fear.
Students at nearby Lady Shri Ram College have also highlighted poorly lit roads, limited police presence and gaps in surveillance around the campus.
The concerns are not confined to one neighborhood or one city.
In Bihar state’s Jamui district, a video showing the sexual assault of a teenage girl and the beating of her male friend triggered widespread anger last month. Police arrested three minors and formed a special investigation team.
Elsewhere in Bihar, a woman was allegedly raped and brutally assaulted in a hotel room on Sunday after travelling to the Begusarai district for work. A video of the assault later circulated on social media.
Punjab’s Lovely Professional University (LPU) suspended classes and postponed mid-term examinations after a protest over an alleged rape turned violent on Sunday with protesters clashing with the police and vandalism being reported.
Across India, sexual violence is a ​major issue, with more than 80 rapes reported to police every day, according to data from the National Crime Records Bureau.
Women’s rights groups, including People Against Rape in India (Pari), have long argued that official crime statistics do not capture the full scale of sexual violence because many assaults go unreported.
The gang rape and murder of a student in New Delhi in 2012 sparked nationwide protests and led to sweeping legal reforms, including tougher penalties for offenders and the creation of fast-track courts.
But the changes have done little to reduce sexual violence. Women’s rights groups say entrenched patriarchal attitudes, understaffed police forces and delays in the justice system leave many perpetrators believing they can avoid punishment.
“Women’s safety is non-negotiable. Women must be safe on every street, at every hour,” said Delhi Lieutenant Governor Taranjit Singh Sandhu, while ordering the creation of a dedicated “Pink Force” of women personnel to enhance the safety of women and children in education establishments, metro stations and other locations across New Delhi. The Supreme Court has now stepped in. On September 28, it took up the recent sexual assault cases on its own initiative and said they raised serious concerns about the way authorities were protecting women in public spaces.
The apex court has directed Delhi Police to identify vulnerable locations, improve patrolling and conduct audits of lighting and CCTV coverage in parks and other public spaces.
But Yashvardhan Azad, a retired senior police officer, says the problem starts well before the police are called.
“The failure is first the society where any woman going alone at night or with a friend is viewed with suspicion,” Azad told DW. “The political climate in many states favor moral policing.”
“Public places are neglected and badly lit. Police can never be everywhere. Most importantly, recent cases reveal the municipality’s failure. Well-lit roads, better managed parks and trained guards are the answer, along with CCTVs,” he said.
Kalpana Vishwanath of Jagori, a Delhi-based women’s rights group, says cities “must be designed and built to be inherently safe, inclusive and gender responsive.”
“Evaluating public spaces on nine infrastructure and social parameters, including lighting, clear walkways, transit access, crowds, the presence of women and security personnel, and natural surveillance from vendors and shops, would make them safer and go a long way in curtailing sexual violence,” Vishwanath told DW.
Criminal lawyer Rebecca John said police cannot be everywhere at all times but the failures continue once a case reaches them for investigation, with seizures improperly made and witness statements badly recorded.
“Many times, the police refuse to register a case because they are inclined to disbelieve the woman at the very beginning,” John told DW.
She also pointed to delays in forensic examination, emphasizing that India has just seven Central Forensic Science Laboratories, alongside 32 state and 97 regional labs, adding to the time needed to process crucial evidence, often leading to acquittals or overturned rulings in higher courts.
The Supreme Court has given Delhi Police four weeks to complete audits and put stepped up patrols in place.
Whether that restores the confidence students describe losing will be tested well beyond the deadline, in the public spaces where many women continue to weigh every journey against concerns for their safety.

item.title: Nepal’s grim DNA puzzle to identify flood dead
item.description:
Clutching a photograph of his missing son, Rajesh Ram is pinning his hopes on DNA testing -- like thousands of others desperately seeking relatives swept away by Nepal’s catastrophic Himalayan floods.
“I searched for him everywhere, but I could not find his body,” 53-year-old Ram told AFP, still waiting for answers about his son Suroj Kumar, a garage mechanic in Betrawati, which was swamped by the floods.
Nepal was overwhelmed by the sheer scale of destruction from the tsunami-like wall of freezing water and debris triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on the Nepal-China border on August 26.
The scale of the identification task is immense.
With thousands of DNA profiles to process, fragmented remains and limited technical capacity and manpower, experts warn matching bodies to families could take weeks.
Nepali disaster authorities have recovered 1,454 bodies -- but around a third of those are only partial remains.
Just 112 bodies have been identified and returned to their families. A further 5,285 people are missing in Nepal, including hundreds of foreigners.
In China, the toll is 43 dead and 519 missing, according to state media -- taking the combined toll to nearly 1,500 dead and 5,800 missing.
At Nepal’s two forensic laboratories, both in Kathmandu, experts are working to profile samples and build a database on a scale they have never handled before.
“In a year we would analyze 1,000-1,500 samples, often in case of paternity or crime scenes,” said Mukul Pradhan, chief scientific officer at the National Forensic Science Laboratory. “We are now processing thousands of samples.”
A total of 3,685 forensic samples are undergoing DNA testing, including more than 1,300 collected from recovered bodies.
Blood samples are easier to profile, but those taken from teeth or bones can take several days to process.
Nepal has buried more than 1,200 bodies, carefully numbering and tagging them so they can be retrieved if a DNA match is found.
“A large number of people are missing, and the bodies that have been found they are difficult to identify,” said Nepali police spokesman Abi Narayan Kafle. “We understand the pain people are in, and our teams are working diligently.”
Some bodies were carried far downstream by the floodwaters, further complicating the task, said Nirajan Thapa , Chief of Biology section at the National Forensic Science Laboratory.
“In an earthquake or an accident, people are recovered in a specific area, so we work in a closed scenario -- the body’s DNA has to be compared to a limited number of samples,” Thapa said. “But that scale has now become very large.”
DNA alone cannot identify a body without a reference sample from a relative.
“Just by extracting a DNA profile is not enough to identify someone,” Thapa said. “We have to extract a DNA profile from their relatives and then compare.”
That means authorities must process samples from both unidentified remains and thousands of relatives before they can establish matches.
Several countries have sent in support teams, including neighboring India and China, as well as South Korea. Fingerprint experts from the United States and Singapore are also assisting.
Thapa said that with that help, matching could begin within a few weeks.
But until the results come, the families behind those samples face a painful limbo. Some families have held symbolic cremation funerals for the missing.
Ram wonders if he will ever get any answers. “I am waiting if I can find any remains of my son,” he said.

item.title: ‘Cockroaches’ join India protests demanding election chief resign
item.description:
Indian protesters rallied in New Delhi and Mumbai on Friday, including members of the popular youth-led “cockroach” party, demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner over alleged voter-roll irregularities.
Police deployed in large numbers as protesters waved the national flag and chanted slogans against the Election Commission of India (ECI), demanding its chief Gyanesh Kumar step down.
A newspaper investigation by The Indian Express last month alleged impropriety during a large-scale voter-roll revision that has struck millions of names from lists.
The ECI, India’s constitutional body responsible for conducting elections, has rejected allegations of wrongdoing, while Kumar has not commented.
Hundreds of people gathered on roads around Jantar Mantar, a government-designated protest site in the heart of New Delhi, which was sealed off behind police barricades.
“My motivation is our future,” 19-year-old protester Nidhi Sharma, a Delhi University student, told AFP. “I have to vote.”
Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party -- which began in May as a satirical online movement -- meanwhile rallied in Mumbai’s Shivaji Park, in their first protests since July, when their nationwide campaign helped oust the education minister.
Opposition politicians have accused the ECI of acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
At the Delhi protest, Mina Giri, 38, said her name had been removed from the rolls even though she has lived in the capital for 15 years and voted in previous elections.
“How could my fundamental right be taken away from me?” she said.
Another protester, Imran, 18, said his family had been left off the list.
“Because of this, we are struggling to get our other official documents,” preventing them from receiving government benefits, he said.
“We are poor, don’t have a lot and are dependent on it.”
Police detained multiple protesters in Delhi, put them on buses and dropped them off elsewhere, but some returned to the Jantar Mantar site on foot.
“No matter how many times they do this, we are going to return and protest,” said Sahana, an advocate who was picked up by police but then walked back two kilometers (a mile) to rejoin the demonstration.
“You cannot take away our right to walk, can you?” she said.
Mobile internet services were also suspended in the area.
Some opposition politicians who joined the protest were briefly detained by police.
Opposition parties have also announced plans for more protests, including a march to the Election Commission in New Delhi on Tuesday and “Save Democracy” rallies countrywide in the days following.
Activist Vijeta Dahiya, who was involved in the previous “cockroach” campaign against the education minister, said that “no one wants to protest, but are forced to raise their voice when the government makes mistakes.”
“Protest anywhere in the country,” he said. “It is a matter of a right to vote.”

item.title: Hundreds of French high schools shut as new violence erupts
item.description:
French high school students lit fires outside schools and faced off with police on Friday as a protest movement that has forced the closure of some 400 establishments showed no sign of abating.
The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils at lycees in their final years of schooling block access to buildings and clash with police.
The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions inadequate including overheated classrooms, and that there are too many staff absences.
The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it has described as “urban violence.”
Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing tear gas canisters to disperse the protests.
In Paris on Friday, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools -- Leonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the southeast -- with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said “the high school student movement is being held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups,” adding that nearly 400 high schools out of the 3,700 in the country were expected to be closed on Friday.
Many high schools have also planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille.
At least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement, Geffray told BFMTV. Some 170 students have been wounded while over 100 high schools have suffered “severe damage.”
“Parents must clearly step up and tell their children not to go” to the protests, he added. “What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger.”
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said he has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children during the protests and “pay for repairs.”
Since the start of the movement, around 2,000 people have been taken into police custody “90% of whom were minors,” Darmanin told RTL.
In the western city of Rennes, the tension was already palpable outside the Jean-Mace high school with students dressed in black and wearing balaclavas standing not far from a heavy police presence.
“As far as we’re concerned, we’ve won -- our school is closed this morning,” said Lola, 16, who declined to give her last name.
She condemned what she said was police violence. “It makes us even angrier -- the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us.”
Police used tear gas at the Kerichen high school in Brest, in western France, an AFP photographer said.
The protests have also made a strong political echo just over half a year before presidential elections, with the government accusing the hard left France Unbowed (LFI) -- whose firebrand leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is again standing for the presidency -- of being behind the movement.
But senior LFI official Manuel Bompard accused the government of “descending into conspiracy theories.”
In a bid to ease tensions, Geffray said he was Friday meeting with education unions and high school student associations to find common ground for dialogue.

item.title: CUET students continue protest, rally on holiday
item.description:
The movement by teachers, officers, employees and students of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) demanding the reinstatement of Professor Abu Sadat Mohammad Sayem as vice-chancellor continued on Friday, with students staging a protest rally on campus.
The rally began around 2:30pm from in front of the university’s Teachers-Students Centre, passed through several campus roads and ended at the main gate. Students chanted slogans demanding Professor Sayem’s reinstatement.
Since the movement began, students have held various protest programmes, including torch processions, red-card demonstrations, “Why 56?”, “Testimony in White Sarees,” a procession wearing masks depicting the former vice-chancellor, protests with black cloth over their eyes, and a “Protest Concert.”
Zulkarnaine Mihad, a fourth-year student of the Department of Mechanical Engineering who joined the rally, said, “Today marks the 11th day of our movement. No action has yet been taken in response to our demand. Classes and examinations remain suspended. Our movement will continue until our demand is met.”
Students launched the movement the same day, protesting the change just 56 days after Professor Sayem assumed office. They began a “complete shutdown” the following day, September 22.
After 11 days of protests, no resolution has yet been reached over their demand to reinstate Professor Sayem.

bdnews24.com editor-in-chief Toufique Imrose Khalidi dies
item.description:
Toufique Imrose Khalidi, editor-in-chief of online news outlet bdnews24.com, has died. He was 59.

He died while undergoing treatment at a hospital in London on Friday.

According to a report published by bdnews24, Toufique Imrose Khalidi was taken to a London hospital on Thursday night after suffering a brain haemorrhage.

Physicians pronounced him dead at 2:23 pm local time on Friday.

Family said Toufique Imrose Khalidi was in London on a personal trip. He suddenly fell ill there.

Toufique Imrose Khalidi studied in the Department of English at the University of Dhaka and worked as a journalist at The Daily Star and the BBC. He took charge of bdnews24.com in 2006. He had served as the news outlet’s editor-in-chief since then.

The date for bringing his body back to the country has not yet been decided. The family will announce the place and time of his janaza and burial once they are finalised.

News agency BSS adds: President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir expressed profound grief and shock at the death of Toufique Imrose Khalidi.

In a message of condolence, the President prayed for the peace of the departed soul and conveyed his deepest sympathy to the bereaved family.

The President said that Toufique Imrose Khalidi was a pioneer in the development of online and digital journalism in the country. With his death, the nation has lost an experienced, gracious and eminent media personality. His contributions to journalism and the media will be remembered for a long time.

Recalling his personal memories with Toufique Imrose Khalidi, the President said that his death was deeply painful for him. He was profoundly saddened and grieved by Khalidi’s passing.

Legal hurdles, manpower shortages hamper crackdown on teen gangs
item.description:
Legal complications, manpower shortages and inadequate infrastructure are making it difficult for police to tackle the growing menace of teenage gangs, with restrictions on how juvenile offenders can be prosecuted and detained posing a particular challenge, according to senior police officials.
Under the Children Act 2013, offenders aged 18 or below must be sent to juvenile development centres and cannot be tried by mobile courts or in regular courts or kept in jail in the same manner as adults, the officials said.
They also pointed to administrative difficulties in maintaining specialized training for officers handling juvenile offenders. Officers trained to deal with such cases may later be transferred or assigned to other duties, making it difficult to maintain institutional capacity.
DMP Additional Police Commissioner Mohammad Osman Gani (Crime and Operations) told Dhaka Tribune recently that a lack of family education was a major reason behind juvenile crime.
“Parents need to know where their children go after leaving home in the evening. If parents become more aware, juvenile crime will gradually decline,” he said.
He said children and juveniles could not be dealt with through mobile courts, tried in regular courts or kept in jail in the same manner as adults, placing greater responsibility on families to prevent juvenile crime.
The challenges have come under renewed scrutiny following the recovery of the body of 13-year-old Ishayat Shahriar alias Opratim in Comilla on September 20.
Since then, law enforcement agencies have reportedly been arresting 200–300 teenage gang members almost daily as part of ongoing drives.
So far, 1,672 people have been detained or arrested in Comilla during operations against teenage gangs and local troublemakers, according to the latest available information.
Earlier, on April 12, Emon Hossain alias Alex Emon, leader of the Mohammadpur-based “Alex Group” and an accused in 18 criminal cases, was hacked to death in public. Top criminal Imam ul Hasan Helal alias Pichchi Helal was named as an accused in the murder case.
On September 15, Farhad, who allegedly led the “Patali Group” under Pichchi Helal’s direction, was shot and hacked to death inside a saloon in Arshinagar, Keraniganj.
The teenage gang culture has become increasingly entrenched in Dhaka and other parts of the country in recent years. While the identities of underworld godfathers and criminals are often known, those allegedly providing patronage to teenage gangs largely remain beyond the reach of law enforcement.
Operating under various names, these gangs have spread fear across neighbourhoods. Their members are allegedly involved in establishing territorial dominance, theft, mugging, extortion, drug dealing and even murder over trivial disputes. Some gangs also use social media pages to announce attacks on rival groups.
According to DMP sources, more than half of the members on its list of criminal gangs are aged 20 or below, with around one in six under the age of 18.
The DMP list contains information on 122 active gangs in the capital. Mirpur has the highest number of gangs, while Mohammadpur leads in terms of violence.
Of the 893 gang members whose ages are recorded, 152, or 17%, are under 18, while 322, or 36%, are aged between 18 and 20. In total, 474 members, or 53%, are aged 20 or below.
The list identifies extortion, mugging, robbery, eve-teasing, drug dealing and contract killings among the gangs' criminal activities. The gangs allegedly receive political patronage and support from notorious criminals.
Social and crime experts say teenagers are increasingly becoming involved in serious crimes, with underworld criminals and politically influential groups allegedly using them to carry out criminal activities.
They say influential individuals recruit teenagers for drug dealing, illegal occupation and other offences. Impressionable teenagers, encouraged by local or political patronage, become involved in crime to demonstrate their power.
The growing gang culture has also left parents increasingly worried about their adolescent children.
At a meeting at Police Headquarters on Tuesday, Inspector General of Police Ali Hossain Fakir said a criminal's only identity was that of a criminal and that drug dealers, terrorists and extortionists must be brought to justice.
“There is no scope for considering political identity in this regard,” he said, adding that appropriate legal action must also be taken against juvenile offenders.
Reiterating the police's zero-tolerance policy towards drugs, the police chief stressed the need to ensure public participation through community policing.
Zakaria Zaman, a Class X student at Mohammad Preparatory School and College on Iqbal Road, is regularly accompanied to and from school by his mother, Shirin Akhter.
“I have no end to my worries about my son. Since we live in Mohammadpur, the fear is greater. I spend much of the day taking him to school and tuition classes because I am afraid he might fall into bad company,” she told Dhaka Tribune.
She said juvenile crime was increasing and urged the government to take stronger measures to protect children.
“If juvenile crime cannot be contained, all our efforts will fail,” she said.
Afreen Begum, mother of Md Abdullah, a Class VII student at Dhanmondi Government Boys’ High School, said she now kept a close watch on her son.
“We are very worried about our children, so I keep an eye on him. I also make sure he does not become friends with bad company. The Comilla incident has increased our fears,” she said, urging parents to remain vigilant about their children's friends and whereabouts.
A 2025 survey by the Department of Narcotics Control (DNC) found that around 8.3 million people in Bangladesh were addicted to drugs.
According to the survey, most drug users were men, with 7.76 million male and 285,000 female addicts. It also estimated that 255,000 children and adolescents were addicted to drugs.
Md Manzurul Islam, deputy director and researcher at the DNC Chittagong Metro (South), told Dhaka Tribune that children were being used to commit various crimes, including carrying yaba pills inside their bodies and transporting drugs.
“Children are less likely to be suspected and can be used for lower wages. Many become addicted after being recruited as drug carriers,” he said.
He said some parents took their children along when carrying or trafficking drugs to avoid attracting the attention of law enforcement agencies. Exposure to such activities could gradually normalise drug use and lead to addiction among children.
Drug abuse was another major factor behind the rise in juvenile crime, he said, adding that the limited scope for taking strong legal action against children also contributed to the problem.
Dhaka University Associate Professor Dr Towohidul Haque told Dhaka Tribune that poverty, inadequate family and social education, and drug abuse were driving the spread of teenage gangs across the country.
He said police operations alone would not be enough to address the crisis. Those financing criminal activities, operating drug networks and providing political patronage must be brought to justice, while families, educational institutions and local communities need to strengthen preventive measures.
He said police had been unable to remain fully active in the field since August 5 and had faced attacks while conducting operations in some areas.
He called for coordinated action against teenage gangs and stressed the need for political leaders to play a stronger role in combating crime and maintaining law and order.

item.title: The palace paid in fish: Discovering the ruins of Dubalhati Rajbari
item.description:
It was the peak of the summer season in 2024. Having just wrapped up a business trip, I found myself with some time to spare in the northwestern district of Naogaon. Amidst the hot and sultry weather, I wondered where I could make a quick heritage trip without venturing too far. Some six kilometers southwest of the main township, a near-ruined royal palace emerged as the ideal escapade for a few somber, after-work moments.
Visiting Dubalhati Rajbari offered a profound opportunity to admire a nearly 250-year-old Zamindar estate, yet it stirred a poignant sorrow for a heritage left to fade into neglect. With its grand neoclassical facade—featuring a massive, multi-tiered entrance dominated by towering Roman-style Corinthian pillars and decorative stucco plasterwork—the palace stands as a significant historical monument showcasing the remnants of 19th-century grandeur.
The grand front facade of the main palace building featuring its famous Corinthian columns and decorative roofline crest. The monumental, fluted columns feature ornate, leaf-like capitals at the top. In the foreground, an official green government signboard notes that the historic estate of the Dubalhati Zamindars is preserved under the Department of Archaeology, making any unauthorized alteration or damage a punishable offense under the antiquities act. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The foundation of this Zamindari was laid during the Mughal era by a salt and molasses merchant named Jagatram Ray. Later, one of his descendants, Raja Krishnanath Ray, secured the formal permanent settlement of the estate from Lord Cornwallis, the colonial administrator who introduced the ‘Permanent Settlement’ (the Zamindari system) in British India in 1793.
Local legend says that because no crops could grow in this marshy ( beel ) region at the time, the landlords paid their annual revenue to the Mughal court in the form of 22 Kahons of Koi fish (climbing perch). In the ancient counting system, a Kahon was made of sub-units: one Kahon equaled 16 Pons , one Pon totaled 20 Gondas , and each Gonda meant four individual units. Doing the math, 22 Kahons equates to exactly 28,160 fish. This means the early founders had to deliver over 28,000 live climbing perch to the Mughal Nawab annually as their land tax.
Learning this fun piece of folklore while glancing at the massive dighi (water reservoir) in front of the dilapidated palace, I noticed the water was still teeming with fish. I thought to myself, no wonder the Zamindars used fish as currency—the bony things must have been in endless supply.
This specific area is part of the long, ground-floor inner veranda characterized by its sequential, terracotta-adorned semi-circular brick arches and heavy wooden ceiling rafters. Photo: Dhaka Tribune This specific area is part of the long, ground-floor inner veranda characterized by its sequential, terracotta-adorned semi-circular brick arches and heavy wooden ceiling rafters. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
According to local history, the estate flourished most during the reign of Raja Haranath Ray, a grandson of Raja Krishnanath Ray. In the 19th century, he expanded the palace complex, dug deep ponds for drinking water, and established a local school in 1864.
However, the structure I was admiring is actually a born-again palace. On June 12, 1897, the catastrophic 8.1 magnitude Great Assam Earthquake completely altered the architectural footprint of the estate, reducing much of it to absolute ruins. Originally, the complex featured dominant four-story residential blocks, with the main building recognized as one of the tallest structures in North Bengal. When the top floors completely collapsed during the tremors, the family was forced to scale down, rebuilding and repairing only up to the second and third levels.
During this post-earthquake restoration, Raja Haranath Ray Chowdhury and his successor heavily integrated colonial British styling. They added the towering Corinthian pillars, an upper floral relief pediment, and European-inspired baroque "wedding cake" design elements. At the very top of the front pediment, the crest of the British Royal Family remains engraved—historically marking a token of special favor granted to the Zamindars.
The ruined grand entry archway leading directly into the inner ceremonial courtyard and the central temple theater area of the Dubalhati Rajbari. The topmost crest features intricate colonial-era floral relief carvings and crown motifs, showing the blend of European and Mughal styles used by the Zamindars. Through the wide gateway, one can see the skeleton of a two-story residential inner block. The plaster has entirely worn away, exposing the core red-brick structure, hollowed-out window sockets, and crumbling archways. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Originally, the complex boasted over 300 rooms organized sequentially around seven inner courtyards designed to balance natural light with royal privacy. The core residential block, known as the Baro Dalan , once rose three to four stories high. Closer to the outer wings sat the Royal Kachhari , which served as the feudal courtroom and administrative office where the Zamindars and their ministers managed the sprawling estate and collected revenues. The complex also featured an ornate open pavilion designated for cultural entertainment and religious festivals, where classical music soirees, dance performances, and traditional Jatra (folk theatre) were regularly staged.
Following the abolition of the Zamindari system in 1950, the royal family relocated to India, leaving the palace abandoned. Today, the structure is severely dilapidated. The plasterwork has stripped away entirely, exposing the underlying bare bricks, and the flooring has degraded back to natural soil and debris over decades of neglect. Large portions of the upper floors and the western wing of the Baro Dalan have completely collapsed. One has to be extremely cautious when walking near or inside the crumbling rooms, as parts of the roofs and walls are highly prone to caving in.
The large royal dighi of Dubalhati palace complex. It’s located on the northern (front) side near the main entry. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
As I walked out of that now-silent, once-vibrant royal palace of yesteryears, I stood for a few moments on the bank of the adjacent grand pond. Gazing at the water, the soft splash of fish broke the surface, perfectly mirroring the last, crumbling vestiges of a bygone Zamindari.

item.title: JCI Dhaka Sparks signs strategic partnership with Gold’s Gym Bangladesh
item.description:
JCI Dhaka Sparks signed a strategic Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Gold’s Gym Bangladesh on behalf of JCI Bangladesh.
The official signing ceremony took place at Gold’s Gym Bangladesh’s Bashundhara R/A premises, marking a significant milestone in fostering health, fitness, and active lifestyles among youth leaders and organization members.
The agreement was formally signed by Raihan Ahmed Dip, 2026 local president of JCI Dhaka Sparks, on behalf of JCI Bangladesh.
The ceremony was graced by leaders from JCI Bangladesh, including Shahmina Isha Mannan, 2026 national executive vice president; Towfiq Hasan, 2026 national vice president; and Farjana Islam, 2026 local president of JCI Dhaka Metro, alongside key members and advisors of JCI Dhaka Sparks.
Representing Gold’s Gym Bangladesh were Anisul Islam Boby, general manager; Golam Moula Mahi, executive (sales & marketing); and Sadia Choudhury, sr. executive (sales & marketing).
Under this partnership, JCI members and leadership segments will receive exclusive corporate wellness benefits across Gold, Silver, and Pool & Spa packages.
Key highlights of the package include a flat 60% discount for leadership segments (national governing body members, local presidents, and advisory council members/past leaders) and a flat 55% discount for general JCI members.
Additionally, members will receive two weeks of free personal training with certified experts, complimentary physiotherapy and nutritional consultations, and customized fitness and diet blueprints.
This 12-month collaboration aims to build a robust bridge between professional leadership development and physical wellbeing.

item.title: Corporate Amateur Premier League 2026 (Season 4) from October 16
item.description:
With the trophy unveiled, the captains assembled and eight teams ready to compete, the Corporate Amateur Premier League (CAPL) 2026 is set to return for its fourth season, beginning October 16 and running through December.
The season officially moved into its final build-up phase with the CAPL 2026 Captains’ Meet and Trophy Unveiling ceremony, held at Shinepukur Suites, bringing together representatives of all eight participating teams ahead of the tournament.
The event was attended by Mohammed Ashique Rahman, president, CAPL; Rafsun A Jan, general secretary, CAPL; Tarif Mohammed Khan, adviser, CAPL; and Tauhidur Rahman, head of the CAPL umpire panel and first-class umpire of the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB).
The fourth edition will feature eight teams from across the corporate and professional community: Bangladesh Lawyers Cricket Club, Advocates Cricket Club, Lawyers Cricket Association of Bangladesh, Cricket Magnet, Eastern Bank PLC, Bdjobs.com, Fiber@Home, and Renegade Rangers.
The teams have been divided into two groups of four through a lottery draw.
The opening phase will follow a round-robin format, with every team playing three group-stage matches.
The tournament then splits into four knockout pathways: Cup, Bowl, Plate and Bronze ensuring that every team has five matches across the competition.
The tournament will be played over 40 overs, under ICC rules, with matches officiated by BCB senior umpires and scorers.
The 2026 edition will be staged at Fans Cricket Academy Field, Silicon City, Amin Bazar, which will serve as the home of all matches this season.
The tournament's rules also place clear boundaries around player eligibility.
Participants must be at least 28 years old, while players from the Dhaka League, Premier League and Zila League are not eligible under the tournament regulations.
Lawyer teams have an additional qualification requirement, with players required to hold a recognized law degree from Bangladesh or abroad.
President of CAPL Mohammed Ashique Rahman said: “CAPL has been built around a simple idea: bring professionals together through cricket while retaining the competitive character of organized tournament play. With the spirit of sportsmanship and everyone’s support, CAPL will be the north star on the horizon of corporate cricket.”
Adviser of CAPL Tarif Mohammed Khan said: “As we enter the fourth season of CAPL, it is encouraging to see the tournament continue to grow in both participation and competitive spirit. The captains’ meet and trophy unveiling have set the tone, and now the real excitement begins on the field. I wish all eight teams the very best for the season, and I hope CAPL 2026 gives us not only great cricket, but also great stories, friendships and memories beyond the boundary.”

item.title: President: Khalidi’s contributions to journalism will be long remembered
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Friday expressed deep shock and grief at the death of prominent journalist Toufique Imrose Khalidi saying his contributions to journalism and mass media will be remembered for a long time.
In a condolence message released from Bangabhaban, the President prayed for the eternal peace of the departed soul and conveyed his heartfelt sympathy to the bereaved family members.
President Mirza Fakhrul described Khalidi as a pioneer in the development of online and digital journalism in Bangladesh.
“With his passing, the nation has lost an experienced, courteous, and distinguished media personality," the President said.
Recalling his personal memories with Khalidi with deep respect, the President said the demise of the veteran journalist is profoundly painful and heartbreaking for him personally.
The condolence message was communicated by Md. Sarwar Alam, Press Secretary to the President.
Toufique Imrose Khalidi, Editor-in-Chief and Publisher of bdnews24.com, died in London on Friday. He was 59.
He was admitted to St Bartholomew's Hospital in London on Thursday night after suffering a brain haemorrhage, according to the news portal.
Doctors pronounced him dead at 2:23pm local time on Friday, it said.

item.title: 3 held with Vishnu statue, stone fragments in Rangpur
item.description:
Three alleged members of an idol-smuggling ring were arrested and a 15.1kg black stone statue of Hindu deity Vishnu was recovered during a drive in the South Guptapara area of Rangpur city on Thursday night.
Four black stone fragments weighing 6.8 kg in total were also recovered during the operation, Biplob Kumar Goswami, senior assistant director (Media) of Special Response Battalion (SRB)-13, said on Friday morning.
The arrestees are Mizan, 42, of Guptapara, Mozaffar Hossain, 37, of Nayabazar village under Haragach Police Station, and Majedul Islam, 29, of Sonaton Siddik Bazar village under Kaunia Police Station.
According to SRB-13, a team raided a first-floor flat of a four-storey building owned by AKM Humayun Kabir in South Guptapara following a tip-off.
The team recovered the Vishnu statue and four stone fragments and arrested the three alleged members of the smuggling ring.
The arrestees, recovered statue and other seized items were handed over to the police station concerned for further legal action. A case was also filed against the arrestees, the SRB-13 said.

item.title: Dulu: Maize Square to be symbol of Lalmonirhat
item.description:
Disaster Management and Relief Minister Asadul Habib Dulu on Friday said Maize Square in the heart of the district town will become a symbol of Lalmonirhat as maize has emerged as a branding crop of the district.
Maize cultivation has increased significantly in this district. It has now become the main cash crop of Lalmonirhat. The lives of farmers in the region have changed through maize cultivation, bringing smiles to their faces, he said.
Therefore, the heart of the district town has been named Maize Square to highlight the crop’s growing importance to the local economy, he said while addressing a gathering after inaugurating the construction work of the Maize Square in the district town.
The square will be developed with an iconic architectural design. Just as India Gate in Delhi and Faisal Mosque in Islamabad, the Maize Square will become a symbol of Lalmonirhat, he said.
Abul Kasem of Hatibandha upazila has been cultivating maize since 1991, when yields were low and farmers showed little interest in the crop, the minister said, adding, over the past three decades, the scenario has been changed remarkably. Now all farmers in that village cultivate maize.
The soil in the area is suitable for maize cultivation, while farmers are getting satisfactory yields and good prices for their produce, he said.
Small agro-based industries are also being established centering maize production, which has generated hope among people to tale forward the region, Dulu said.
Lalmonirhat Deputy Commissioner Rashedul Hoque Prodhan, Zilla Parishad Administrator AKM Mominul Haque, government officials and political leaders were present on the occasion.

item.title: From colonial history to high fashion: Maheen Khan rewrites Bengal’s textile story in London
item.description:
This year my presence at the London Fashion Week SS2027 was definitely more impactful than the previous year.
It was a six-month project. While researching for this collection I wanted to include three different facets for design development: historical context, heritage textiles, and authenticity of styles.
My collection was inspired by the Bengal Sultanate, followed by Mughal Bengal -- a period of great transformation regionally.
This collection celebrates our Islamic heritage and the styles of the aristocracy.
In popular Sufi philosophy of the medieval era, unadorned white cotton was upheld as a fabric symbolizing humility, spiritual purity, and egalitarianism, which subtly tempered the otherwise opulent displays of royal authority.
The elite and rulers of the Bengal Sultanate 1342–1576 blended Persian Islamic court attire with indigenous lightweight textiles, reflecting both political prestige and the pious, simple aesthetic favored in Sufi traditions based on our cultural ancestry.
In Sufism, the outward aesthetic is deeply tied to inward spiritual states, where minimalism serves as a tool for purifying the soul.
Maheen Khan’s designs being showcased at London Fashion Week SS27. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Hence the styles were mostly chosen in traditional period cuts as documented in museum archives, while a few were blended with more contemporary line of attire.
My key and fundamental style ideas displayed wearability and comfort.
My presentation is inspired by Mul Mul Khaas: the “Legendary Dhaka Muslin” that has very profound historical significance.
It is not possible to produce the finest quality muslin and make it viable for a niche audience. I have used 200 count hand spun hand-woven material.
Superb and wearable handloom developed in same way as the earliest cotton muslin but more affordable and viable for both local and international markets.
The ancient process of making of Dhaka muslin was rooted in a complex 16-step method rather than literal magic, though its unbelievable lightness and transparency inspired legendary myths.
Spun by highly skilled artisans often working near humid river conditions or on boats achieving thread counts to over 1,000.
Today through government initiatives, Dhaka muslin is being revived experimentally in small quantities. Although the cost incurred is high, it is a beginning of a great textile journey.
Maheen Khan’s designs being showcased at London Fashion Week SS27. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
In the same light this collection aims to advocate for high-end sustainable fashion that is slow and valued for being made in Bangladesh.
The traditional Mul Mul Khaas is being revived today through training and skill development. The local design industry is campaigning for better results to protect the textile craft.
This highly skilled and advanced handmade weave reached its absolute zenith during the Mughal era, when Emperors and the gentries of courts like Lucknow and Delhi favored it because it allowed complex undergarments to shine through while keeping the wearer cool in the intense subcontinental heat.
This special and wonderful quality is appreciated by buyers even today something that can be nurtured for the intense heat anywhere especially in the western hemisphere.
This Dhaka muslin is no longer an endangered craft and slowly the steps are being engineered to fulfill slow productions responsibly.
With more exposure to international platforms and sustainable shows we hope to find avenues for handloom and conscious fashion in flourishing global markets.
